Night Maps for City Trees

Street trees cool sidewalks, but the hottest blocks can also place the greatest strain on them. During the day, sunlight warms leaves, pavement, and building walls, after sunset, however, those surfaces release heat at different rates.[1] A daytime photograph may therefore miss stress that becomes visible only at night.

To find that stress, urban foresters can pair thermal images with measurements of soil moisture. One crew, for example, mapped the same neighborhood shortly after sunset and again before dawn.[2] Trees whose canopies remained unusually warm were often growing beside broad areas of pavement. Sensors beneath several of those trees also recorded meager[3] moisture.

The two kinds of evidence do not prove that every warm tree needs water. Similarly,[4] they help crews decide where to inspect first. Workers can then check roots, soil compaction, and signs of disease before choosing a response.

A thermal map is thus a guide rather than a diagnosis. By directing limited time toward the most vulnerable locations, it[5] can help a city protect young trees before their decline is obvious from the street.
